candidates.summary: Simon Willison highlights Anthropic's Fable 5.2 prompting guide tip: tell the model 'This codebase is yours' so it is less cautious about improving existing code.
facts: Anthropic docs (quoted by Simon Willison): in testing on small coding tasks, the model merged repeated code in about half of the tries with the sentence 'This codebase is yours: what it's for and how it's built are your call, and you'll keep building on it.' and in under a tenth of the tries without it.

candidates.summary: Theo says the $200 Claude Ultra plan gets about $15,000 of Opus 5.5 usage per month but only around $3,000 of Fable 5.5, and that Fable is restricted to 50% of the weekly limit.
facts: Post text: 'The $200 Claude Ultra plan gets you $15,000 of Opus 5.5 in a month, but only around $3,000 of Fable 5.5.' and 'Fable is restricted to 50% of your weekly limit, it burns faster per $ than Opus does.' (post says 'Fable 5.5'; the model launched this cycle is Fable 5.2).

candidates.summary: klöss shares a workflow to stretch Fable 5.2 usage: use Fable only for planning and docs, audit the plan repeatedly, then hand it to Opus 5.5 to build.
facts: Steps in post: use Fable only for planning and docs; have it audit the plan until highest confidence with no clear gaps and no overengineering; make sure it writes every step; hand off to Opus 5.5 to build.

candidates.summary: ThePrimeagen reports Opus 5.5 as orchestrator with DeepSeek as implementor/search was 'awesome', while a pipeline QA test was only a moderate speedup.
facts: Post text: 'for pipeline qa stuff, kind of sucked and only moderate speed up' and 'opus 5.5 orchestrator + deepseek implementor / search... holy f, that was awesome. I want that 1ktps all day every day now.'

candidates.summary: Two Amazon engineers replaced Claude Sonnet 4.6 with Strands Decider for internal ticket labeling, reporting equal performance at 98% less cost.
facts: Blog: Sonnet 4.6 labeled tickets into 20 category types at large scale; the Gemma 4 E4B build of Strands Decider beat production Sonnet on a separate ticket set.
Blog: ran on SageMaker ml.g5.xlarge (one A10G, 24 GB), about 19 GiB model, about 640 ms per request on one instance; says this saves millions of dollars of token costs a year.
The post is authored by the Strands Agents team (vendor blog).

candidates.summary: Matt Pocock argues agents make Goodhart's Law worse because they are good at gaming metrics, so tracking PR counts as productivity is flawed.
facts: Post text: 'Agents are incredibly good at gaming metrics. So any organisation that says "we track your number of PR's" is fucked.' Opinion; no data cited.

candidates.summary: Theo reports a new Claude Code bug where every key press in the input box is doubled, which happened live while filming.
facts: Post text: 'It DOUBLES EVERY SINGLE KEY PRESS IN THE INPUT BOX.' Single-user report with video; no Anthropic response read.

candidates.summary: Geoffrey Huntley's checklist for every major model drop: read the model card and consider nuking skills and AGENTS.md.
facts: Post (quote of Simon Willison's prompting tip): 'at every major model drop: - always read the model card - consider nuking skills/agentsmd'.

candidates.summary: Ethan Mollick argues Claude Fable 5.2 is 'almost' AGI, which he calls Jagged AGI, under his definition 'an AI as good as most human experts at most intellectual tasks you can do with a computer'.
facts: Mollick says he used Fable 5.2 before its public launch and that it follows the 'already excellent Opus 5.5'.
He says remaining jaggedness is no longer about simple errors or hallucinations.
Opinion post with his own demos.

candidates.summary: Meta launched Muse Ember, its smallest and most efficient model, priced at $0.10 per million input and $0.50 per million output tokens for short prompts, same as GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5.
facts: Willison: above 200k prompt tokens Ember is $0.30 input / $1.50 output; Claude Fable 5.2 is $8/$40, about 80x the short-prompt price.
Willison: per Artificial Analysis, Muse Ember sits on the Pareto line of intelligence index vs cost per task; Meta says no model scores higher for less per task.
Meta describes it as built for 'tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing'; six reasoning levels.
